grammar.title: Frase
grammar.rule: em + o → no; em + a → na. O livro está na bolsa. O envelope está no armário.

rows: A chave pequena entra na bolsa.

grammar.note_en:
A contraction joins two words into one written form. Portuguese normally joins em with the definite articles o and a: em + o becomes no, and em + a becomes na. The noun’s grammatical gender determines the article: o café → no café (“in the café”); a mesa → na mesa (“on the table”). The meaning is still location. The indefinite frames from chapter 1 remain em um café (“in a café”) and em uma mesa (“on a table”). These are different reference choices, not alternative spellings of no/na. The story first identifies a table and then calls it the table.

Em does not always mean English “in”: no chão means “on the floor,” na parede means “on the wall,” and na janela can mean “at the window.” Use the scene and the object to interpret the relation. No armário means “in the cupboard” here; na bolsa means “in the bag.” Estar still gives a location or condition, while ser identifies: O nome é Café (“The name is Café”); O envelope está fechado (“The envelope is closed”).

Dentro means “inside,” and fora means “outside.” A container can be supplied by the context: the named bag is open, and O livro está dentro means “The book is inside [it].” Dentro de uma bolsa means “inside a bag.” The reference can later be the café, clearly signalled by entering and leaving; it is not always the bag. Perto de Ana means “near Ana,” and longe de Ana means “far from Ana.” Near and far are relative to the person or object being used as the reference point, not absolute distances.

Procura means “looks for”; encontra means “finds.” Looking does not guarantee finding: Ana procura a chave pequena, “Ana looks for the small key”; Ana encontra a chave pequena, “Ana finds the small key.” Entra means “enters/goes in,” and sai means “leaves/goes out”: Bia entra no café, “Bia enters the café”; Bia sai, “Bia goes out.” A moved object can also be the subject: A chave pequena entra na bolsa means “The small key goes into the bag”; O envelope sai means “The envelope comes out [of the cupboard].” The preceding person’s action supplies who moves it. These are restricted third-person singular frames, not complete conjugations.

Agora means “now,” marking the changed scene; também means “also,” adding another applicable item or person. Só means “only,” limiting what is stated: O armário tem só um envelope, “The cupboard contains only an envelope.” Ou offers alternatives: a chave grande ou a chave pequena, “the large key or the small key.” A label supplies a name; the characters do not learn the contents of Rosa’s letter because they never open the envelope.
